Title:
Objectivity, basis ambiguity, and the classical simulability of concordant quantum computation
Authors:
Bishal Kumar Das
,
Sourav Manna
,
Vaibhav Madhok
View PDF
HTML (experimental)
Abstract:
Concordant quantum computations, in which circuits whose register carries zero quantum discord with respect to every subsystem at every step, contain neither entanglement nor any other form of quantum correlation, yet no efficient classical simulation of them is known beyond restricted gate sets. We argue that the obstruction is not a shortage of correlations but the absence of a uniquely identifiable local product basis, and we develop this \emph{basis ambiguity} on two fronts. Quantitatively, we introduce the Basis Ambiguity Measure $\beta\in[0,1]$, the normalized dimension of the manifold of admissible diagonalizing bases on a gate support, and prove a sharp equivalence: a concordance-preserving gate that defeats the Local Basis Finder of Cable and Browne exists if and only if $\beta>0$. Both directions are constructive. Physically, we identify the resource whose absence the obstruction is: \emph{basis objectivity}, a redundant and independently accessible record of the local basis. We show that an environment in spectrum broadcast form, together with the system--environment interaction map, replaces the NP-hard degeneracy test of Eastin by a fixed number of pairwise fragment comparisons per gate, at a cost independent of register size and circuit depth; the two ingredients live on different axes (state and dynamics), and neither alone suffices. We further prove that a theory in which every state has a strictly unique decomposition into perfectly distinguishable pure states has a simplex state space and lacks the continuity content of Hardy's fifth axiom, so that $\beta$ is a computational witness of that axiom. Finally, as a proof of principle that basis ambiguity carries operational content, we present a concordant encryption protocol with hidden local bases, together with an explicit account of what its security does and does not rest on.

This study presents an experimental demonstration of a novel quantum phenomenon,  termed Operational Quantum Unity (OQU), achieved on noisy intermediate-scale quan tum (NISQ) hardware. Using a variational quantum algorithm, we consistently achieved  near-zero entanglement entropy (approximately 1.44×10−15), a global cost function min imum of zero, and reproducible bitstring clusters across multiple runs without classical  error correction or post-selection. The circuit, composed of minimal gate sequences ap plied to qubit pairs, exhibits deterministic behavior and symmetric optimal parameters  ([1.57,0,1.57,0,1.57,0]). These results, obtained using Qiskit and IBM quantum hard ware, suggest the emergence of a stable quantum information structure, potentially indica tive of a hypothesized quantum soliton or novel quantum state. A comprehensive set of  metrics– fidelity, purity, entropy, and measurement counts– were analyzed to confirm the  reproducibility and stability of the observed phenomenon. As a preprint, these findings  have not undergone peer review and should not be considered conclusive without further  validation. This work, completed as of 06:12 PM on Monday, May 19, 2025, establishes a  significant milestone in exploring noise-resilient quantum states on NISQ devices.

published: 2026-10-07T11:06:02Z
summary: There exist two different paradigms for records in isolated quantum systems: decoherent histories (which determines which past events leave formal records) and quantum Darwinism (which determines which current events get redundantly recorded). Neither one implies the other, and connections between the two are scarcely investigated. We unify quantum Darwinism and decoherent histories based on the insight that only redundant records about past events matter. The resulting framework of past redundancy encompasses quantum Darwinism when applied to events at the current time, and it connects redundancy to decoherence of histories and the probability sum rule via the Bhattacharyya coefficient (or fidelity). Importantly, various examples show that past redundancy is a more widespread phenomenon than the fine-tuned models necessary for quantum Darwinism suggest.
